input.command: ls -R src; cat -n src/store.ts; cat -n src/routes.ts
input.description: List source files and show store and routes

input.command: grep -rn "system\|buildRoutes\|deleteRepo\|isAdmin\|user\b\|req.user\|owner" --include=*.ts . | grep -v node_modules | head -50; ls -a; ls test tests 2>/dev/null
input.description: Search for callers and system owner references

input.command: cat -n src/git-auth.ts src/config.ts src/api.ts | head -120; cat package.json
input.description: Show repo type, config, and api files

input.reason: Both findings are confirmed. In src/store.ts:29, `Store.deleteRepo` handles non-admin callers with `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')`. This matches rows owned by the caller and also every row whose owner is `system`, so any non-admin can delete system-owned repos. The only thing that separates callers is `ctx.isAdmin` at line 25, and it only selects the unrestricted admin path. In src/routes.ts:26-33, the `deleteRepo` route passes `req.params.id` and `req.user` straight to `store.deleteRepo` with no ownership or role check of its own. It returns 204 when the delete succeeds. I looked for anything that would block this and found nothing: no middleware, no other callers of `buildRoutes`, no tests, and no other guard in the repository. `registerRepo` sets `owner: req.user.oid`, so the `'system'` clause is not needed for users to delete their own repos. Its only effect is to let non-owners delete system rows.
input.summary: Non-admin delete filter matches system-owned repos, letting any user delete them

findings.text: The delete route applies no ownership check of its own and relies on `Store.deleteRepo`, whose filter lets a non-admin delete system-owned repositories.
findings.reason: First claim: the route has no ownership check of its own. This holds. At src/routes.ts:26-33 the handler only calls `await store.deleteRepo(req.params.id, req.user);` and maps the result to 204, or to 404 if it throws. It checks neither owner nor role. Second claim: the route relies on `Store.deleteRepo`. This holds, since that call is the handler's only authorization logic. Third claim: the store's filter lets a non-admin delete system-owned repos. This holds. src/store.ts:29 runs `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')` for non-admins, so any row owned by `system` matches whoever the caller is.

findings.text: For a non-admin caller the delete also matches rows whose owner is `system`, so any authenticated user can delete shared system repositories.
findings.reason: First claim: for a non-admin caller the delete also matches rows whose owner is `system`. This holds. src/store.ts:25-29 skips the admin branch and runs `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')`, and the `OR owner = 'system'` clause matches system rows no matter what `ctx.oid` is. Second claim: any authenticated user can delete these repos. This holds. The route at src/routes.ts:28 passes whatever `req.user` the request carries, with no further check, and I found no guard anywhere else in the repo. Because `registerRepo` sets `owner: req.user.oid` (routes.ts:21), system rows are not owned by any individual user, so calling them shared system repositories fits the code.

input.severity_reason: This is an exploitable broken-access-control flaw. Any non-admin caller can send a delete request with the id of a system-owned repo and permanently remove its row, because src/store.ts:29 explicitly matches `owner = 'system'` and neither the store nor the route adds any other check. The result is unauthorized data loss.
